abstract.p: The origins of digital health are open to interpretation. If visualization of internal human anatomy constitutes digitization, then the dawn of digitized health can be traced to Röntgen's X-ray discovery in 1895. Another interpretation relies on electronic medical records, where the origin rests with home-grown systems developed at various medical centers in the 1960's. Much has changed since those early days. Technology has advanced tremendously, as has its role in healthcare. Today, digital health extends far beyond imaging and electronic medical records. It now involves collecting data from a diverse array of sensors and sources, applying privacy-preserving methods for gathering and sharing data and knowledge for both clinical and research purposes, and integrating, presenting, and interpreting health information. Digital health also encompasses treatment recommendation systems and much more. Succinctly stated, technology from our community is improving daily patient care. In the United States, and similarly in other parts of the world, patients interact with the medical community via interconnected entities, namely: medical call centers, nursing staff, and medical doctors of various specialty. Using search, recommendation, and language technology, we address critical resource (staffing and/or equipment) shortages in each of the aforementioned entities either via staff augmentation or simply providing a "second opinion" to overburdened clinicians. Initially, we introduce a commercial system in support of medical call centers. Using conversational search technology, a multilingual chat-bot interacts with patients at the time of their convenience, 24 hours per day, 365 days per year, in the language of their choosing, from within a set of over 100 languages and dialects. This chatbot, after verifying patient identity and obtaining permission to access the patient's personal electronic medical record, provides conventional clinical guidance, supports office and lab appointment scheduling, and answers simple clarification questions. Detailed or uncommon inquiries are routed to human providers. A key objective of this initiative is to alleviate the excessive workload of medical call center staff, allowing them to focus on addressing more complex requests and concerns.
